opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a few things. First, the trajectory. If you look at where 3D generation was just two or three years ago, the results were blobby, low-resolution, with messy topology and textures that didn't really hold up. Today the geometry is much sharper, the textures are far more usable, and we can generate assets in seconds that used to take an artist hours or days. When you see that kind of steady, compounding improvement, it's hard to believe it will suddenly stop.

Second, the remaining problems are well-defined. Things like clean quad topology, good UV layouts, rigging that actually works for animation, part-level structure, and fine-grained controllability. These are hard, but they're not mysterious. Artists know exactly what a "good" asset looks like, and that means we can measure progress, collect the right data, and design the right objectives. A problem you can clearly describe is a problem you can make progress on.

Third, I have a background in computer graphics and physical simulation, and in graphics we've spent decades building tools that encode a lot of structure about how 3D content should behave. Combining that classical knowledge with modern generative models is really powerful. You don't have to learn everything from scratch with brute force; you can bring in priors from geometry processing, from rendering, from simulation.

And finally, there's the feedback loop with users. We have a lot of creators, game developers, 3D printing folks, using Meshy every day, and they tell us very directly what's not good enough yet. That signal is incredibly valuable. It keeps us focused on the problems that actually matter in production rather than just chasing benchmarks.

So I'm optimistic, not because it's easy, but because the problems are concrete, the tools are getting better, and the progress so far has been real. I think the gap between "AI-generated" and "production-ready" is going to keep shrinking, and probably faster than many people expect.

r001.rationale: The response cites rapid improvements over the past two or three years and steady, compounding progress as reasons to expect further technical advances.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention early characters having four faces or separate front, back, left, and right textures being applied to the model.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I'm optimistic because of where the hard problems actually sit now, not because they're easy.

When we started Meshy, the fundamental question was whether you could generate a usable 3D asset from text or an image at all. Not a point cloud, not a blurry blob, but something with geometry you'd actually put in a scene. That was a research question with a real chance of a negative answer. Today it's answered. The models work. What's left is a different kind of problem: topology quality, clean UV layouts, PBR textures that hold up under different lighting, rigging that animators don't have to redo. Those are engineering and data problems, and I've spent most of my career on exactly that category of problem.

My background is in simulation and compilers, Taichi before this. What that taught me is that when a problem is bounded, when you can measure it and iterate on it, it eventually falls. Mesh topology is a good example. Artists complain about triangle soup, and they're right to. But "good topology" is something we can define, score, and train toward. Same with texture consistency across views. These aren't mysteries. They're loss functions we haven't fully written yet.

The second reason is scale. Every month we have more users generating more assets and telling us which ones they kept and which ones they threw away. That feedback loop is the thing that didn't exist for 3D two years ago. Images had billions of training examples. 3D had almost nothing clean. Now the data is being created by the product itself, and the model gets better in a way that compounds.

And third, I'd just say that the hardware and the research community are both moving in our direction. Three years ago I had to argue that 3D generation was a real field. Now it's one of the busiest areas in graphics research, and the papers coming out every month hand us ideas we can ship in weeks.

So will the last ten percent be hard? Yes, very. Getting from "good enough for a prototype" to "a studio ships this without touching it" is a long tail. But I don't see anything on that list that looks impossible. I see a lot of things that look like work, and work is what we do.

r001.rationale: The response points to hardware and research advances, with new papers appearing monthly and ideas reaching the product in weeks, as reasons for confidence.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re solvable because we can see a path to improvement. Generating a 3D model isn’t the same as generating a model that someone can immediately use. You need good geometry, good textures, and enough control to get the result you want. Those are difficult problems, but they’re concrete problems that we can measure and work on.

That doesn’t mean simply making the model bigger will solve everything. We still need better data, better algorithms, and better tools around the model. But I don’t see a fundamental reason those things can’t improve. That’s what makes me optimistic.

r001.rationale: The candidate says there is a path to improvement and describes measurable problems, but does not ground its confidence in the speed of technological progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that we’re not waiting for some new law of physics to be discovered. We can already see that these models can generate useful 3D assets. The remaining challenge is making that quality consistent and giving users more control—getting the geometry, textures, and details to match what they actually want.

Those are difficult problems, but there are concrete things we can improve: the data, the model, and the way we incorporate feedback. We can run experiments and measure whether we’re making progress. That doesn’t mean scaling alone will solve everything, or that we know exactly how long it will take. But there’s a path to keep improving, and that’s what gives me confidence.

r001.rationale: The response cites existing capabilities, concrete avenues for improvement, and measurable experiments, but does not ground confidence in the speed of technological progress.
